In a list of three or more items, put a comma before the "and" or "or" that closes the list.
This comma is called the *serial comma*, or the *Oxford comma*.
With it, the reader sees where each item ends,
and does not have to guess whether the last two items form a pair.

Write "the mean, the median, and the mode",
not "the mean, the median and the mode". <!-- check-serial-comma: allow -->
The same holds when the items are long, are split across source lines, or contain math.

::: {#exm-serial-comma}

## Adding the serial comma

> ❌ We compare the lasso, ridge regression and elastic net. <!-- check-serial-comma: allow -->
>
> ✅ We compare the lasso, ridge regression, and elastic net.

In the first version, a reader can take "ridge regression and elastic net" as a single method that combines the two.
The comma before "and" shows that there are three methods.

:::

A list of two items takes no comma: "the mean and the median".
A phrase that opens a sentence is set off by its own comma, and it does not make a list:
"In practice, the mean and the median agree."

A line that must keep a list without the serial comma, such as a quotation or the ❌ half of an example,
takes the marker `<!-- check-serial-comma: allow -->`.
